    Predictive Modeling

    Last updated on 2026-10-06 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 45 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How does a Random Forest actually make a decision?
    • How well does our model perform on patients it has never seen?
    • Why isn’t accuracy enough in a clinical setting?

    Objectives

    • Explain a Random Forest as a committee of decision trees voting.
    • Train a classifier with .fit() and generate predictions with .predict().
    • Read a confusion matrix and identify the two types of error.
    • Calculate and interpret sensitivity and specificity.

    Where we left off

    This recreates everything from the previous episodes, including the scaled training and test sets. If your Colab session is still running and you’ve already completed these setup steps, you can skip this section. Otherwise, run the following code to recreate the environment:

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sns.set_style("whitegrid")

data = load_breast_cancer()
df = pd.DataFrame(data.data, columns=data.feature_names)
df['diagnosis'] = data.target

X = df[list(data.feature_names)]
y = df['diagnosis']

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

    What a Random Forest actually is

    A decision tree makes a series of simple yes-or-no decisions. For example: “Is the mean radius greater than 15?” If yes, it asks another question, and continues until it reaches a prediction. Decision trees are easy to understand, but a single tree can become too closely tailored to the training data.

    A Random Forest combines many decision trees. Each tree is trained on a slightly different subset of the data, and they vote on the final prediction. The majority vote becomes the model’s answer.

    Using the resident analogy from the first episode, a single decision tree is like asking one resident for an opinion. A Random Forest is like asking a group of residents and going with the majority view, which is usually more reliable than relying on just one person.

    Callout

    People often describe machine learning models as “black boxes”, but a Random Forest is easier to understand than it might seem. It is simply a collection of many decision trees, each making a series of yes-or-no decisions.

    The final prediction comes from combining the votes of all those trees. The model’s complexity comes from having many trees working together, not from any single step being difficult to understand.

    Training the model

    Training the model means letting it learn patterns from the training data. We keep the test set separate so that we can use it later to evaluate how well the model performs on unseen data.

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
rf_model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

    The default of `max_features` changed from `"auto"` to `"sqrt"`.

    Note: the search for a split does not stop until at least one
    valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
    effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features.         		'sqrt'
    max_leaf_nodes max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

    Grow trees with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
    Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
    If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes.         		None
    min_impurity_decrease min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

    A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
    greater than or equal to this value.

    The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

    N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
    - N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

    where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
    samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
    left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

    ``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
    if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

    .. versionadded:: 0.19         		0.0
    bootstrap bootstrap: bool, default=True

    Whether bootstrap samples are used when building trees. If False, the
    whole dataset is used to build each tree.         		True
    oob_score oob_score: bool or callable, default=False

    Whether to use out-of-bag samples to estimate the generalization score.
    By default, :func:`~sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score` is used.
    Provide a callable with signature `metric(y_true, y_pred)` to use a
    custom metric. Only available if `bootstrap=True`.

    For an illustration of out-of-bag (OOB) error estimation, see the example
    :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_ensemble_oob.py`.         		False
    n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

    The number of jobs to run in parallel. :meth:`fit`, :meth:`predict`,
    :meth:`decision_path` and :meth:`apply` are all parallelized over the
    trees. ``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend`
    context. ``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary
    <n_jobs>` for more details.         		None
    verbose verbose: int, default=0

    Controls the verbosity when fitting and predicting.         		0
    warm_start warm_start: bool, default=False

    When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit
    and add more estimators to the ensemble, otherwise, just fit a whole
    new forest. See :term:`Glossary <warm_start>` and
    :ref:`tree_ensemble_warm_start` for details.         		False
    class_weight class_weight: {"balanced", "balanced_subsample"}, dict or list of dicts, default=None

    Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
    If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
    multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
    order as the columns of y.

    Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
    defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
    for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
    [{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
    [{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

    The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
    weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
    as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

    The "balanced_subsample" mode is the same as "balanced" except that
    weights are computed based on the bootstrap sample for every tree
    grown.

    For multi-output, the weights of each column of y will be multiplied.

    Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
    through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified.         		None
    ccp_alpha ccp_alpha: non-negative float, default=0.0

    Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
    subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
    ``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed. See
    :ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
    :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`
    for an example of such pruning.

    monotonic_cst monotonic_cst: array-like of int of shape (n_features,), default=None

    Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.
    - 1: monotonically increasing
    - 0: no constraint
    - -1: monotonically decreasing

    If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

    Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:
    - multiclass classifications (i.e. when `n_classes > 2`),
    - multioutput classifications (i.e. when `n_outputs_ > 1`).

    The constraints hold over the probability of the positive class.

    print("Model trained on", X_train_scaled.shape[0], "patients.")

    OUTPUT 

    Model trained on 398 patients.

    n_estimators=100 means our Random Forest contains 100 decision trees.

    And that’s all it takes to train the model. Notice that training the model required very little code. In many machine learning projects, most of the effort goes into preparing, exploring, and understanding the data before training begins.

    Callout

    We’re using the scaled data to stay consistent with the rest of our workflow. However, Random Forest models do not usually depend on feature scaling, so you would get very similar results if you trained the model on the original X_train data instead.

    Evaluating on unseen patients

    Now it’s time to evaluate the model using the test set, which contains data the model has not seen before.

    PYTHON 

    y_pred = rf_model.predict(X_test_scaled)

    The confusion matrix

    A confusion matrix shows how many predictions were correct and how many were incorrect. It breaks the results into four possible outcomes.

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=[0, 1])  # 0 = Malignant, 1 = Benign

disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
    y_test, y_pred, labels=[0, 1],
    display_labels=['Malignant', 'Benign'], cmap='Blues'
)
plt.title('Confusion Matrix — Test Set')
plt.show()

    Looking at the results from a clinical perspective:

    • Correctly identified a malignant tumour: the model detected cancer correctly.
    • Correctly identified a benign tumour: the model correctly recognised a non-cancerous case.
    • Missed a malignant tumour (false negative): the model incorrectly classified a cancerous tumour as benign.
    • Incorrectly identified a benign tumour as malignant (false positive): the model flagged a non-cancerous tumour as cancerous, potentially leading to additional testing.
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Which error is worse?

    In this clinical setting, which is worse? a false positive or a false negative? Discuss with the person next to you before reading on.

    Many people would argue that a false negative is the more serious mistake in this situation because it means a cancerous tumour was missed, potentially delaying treatment.

    However, a false positive also has consequences. It can lead to unnecessary tests, additional costs, and extra stress for the patient.

    There is no single correct answer. The importance of each type of error depends on the clinical situation and the impact of getting the prediction wrong. The key point is to think about these trade-offs deliberately rather than relying on a model’s default behaviour.

    Can do a debate here with the question.

    Push back gently if the room converges too fast on “false negatives are always worse”: ask what happens to a screening programme with a very high false positive rate.

    Sensitivity and specificity

    Accuracy on its own does not tell the whole story. A model can achieve a high accuracy score while still making mistakes on the cases that matter most.

    That’s why we also look at measures that help us understand the types of errors the model makes:

    PYTHON 

    tp, fn, fp, tn = cm[0, 0], cm[0, 1], cm[1, 0], cm[1, 1]

sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn)   # Of all actual malignant cases, how many did we catch?
specificity = tn / (tn + fp)   # Of all actual benign cases, how many did we correctly clear?

print(f"Sensitivity (catching malignant cases):        {sensitivity:.1%}")

    OUTPUT 

    Sensitivity (catching malignant cases):        90.6%

    PYTHON 

    print(f"Specificity (correctly clearing benign cases):  {specificity:.1%}")

    OUTPUT 

    Specificity (correctly clearing benign cases):  95.3%

    PYTHON 

    print()

    PYTHON 

    print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=['Malignant', 'Benign']))

    OUTPUT 

                  precision    recall  f1-score   support

   Malignant       0.92      0.91      0.91        64
      Benign       0.94      0.95      0.95       107

    accuracy                           0.94       171
   macro avg       0.93      0.93      0.93       171
weighted avg       0.94      0.94      0.94       171
    • Sensitivity — of all the patients who actually have the disease, how many did we correctly catch?
    • Specificity — of all the patients who don’t have the disease, how many did we correctly clear?

    These are simply ways of measuring the balance between false negatives and false positives.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: The dangerously accurate model

    Suppose you are screening for a disease with 1% prevalence, and someone builds a model that simply predicts “healthy” for every single patient.

    What accuracy would it achieve, and what would its sensitivity be?

    It would be 99% accurate. It gets all 99 healthy patients right and only the 1 sick patient wrong.

    Its sensitivity, however, would be 0%: of all the patients who actually have the disease, it catches none of them. The model is worthless despite an impressive-sounding accuracy figure.

    This example shows why accuracy alone can be misleading. In clinical machine learning, we also need to consider the types of mistakes a model makes.

    Key Points
    • A Random Forest is many decision trees, each trained on a random subset, that vote on the final prediction.
    • .fit() trains on the training set; .predict() generates predictions for unseen data.
    • A confusion matrix separates the two kinds of error: false negatives (missed disease) and false positives (false alarms).
    • Sensitivity measures how many true cases you catch; specificity measures how many healthy patients you correctly clear. Accuracy alone can conceal a clinically dangerous model.
